item.title: We’re Asking the Wisconsin Supreme Court to End Warrantless ALPR Searches
item.author: Andrew Crocker
item.content:encoded: Today, EFF joined the ACLU of Wisconsin in filing a petition to the Wisconsin Supreme Court, asking it to rule that the state’s constitution requires a warrant for retrospective searches of ALPR databases used by law enforcement in four cities: Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha, and Green Bay. We represent a religious organization, the Wisconsin Council of Churches, as well as an individual pastor in Green Bay.As the petition explains:Right now, Automated License Plate Readers (“ALPRs”) are recording the movements of vast numbers of Wisconsin drivers as they seek medical care, attend 12-step recovery meetings, attend religious services, participate in protests, attend political meetings, and engage in many other private, sensitive activities. Law enforcement entities throughout Wisconsin collect, store, share, and aggregate this ALPR data. Then they search it, retrospectively tracking the movements of individuals and entire communities in ways that would have been prohibitively costly, if not outright impossible, before the advent of ALPR technology.We all deserve to be free of warrantless mass surveillance. We all deserve to live in a country where surveillance vendors cannot help police upend our system of individualized suspicion. Religious organizations and officials like our clients have a heightened interest in protecting their location privacy because of the range of expressive associations their work entails, including facilitating gatherings for religious worship, as well as offering pastoral care, confidential counseling, and community support. Likewise, the people who visit houses of worship have a strong right to privacy against police monitoring of when they pray, seek addiction counseling, or attend a domestic violence survivor meeting.This is our second lawsuit challenging warrantless ALPR searches, following Earlier this month, a federal court in Oklahoma became the first to rule that ALPRs are a “type of indiscriminate mass surveillance” and suppress evidence from a warrantless ALPR search. We hope the Wisconsin Supreme Court will agree.Read the Wisconsin Supreme Court petition

item.title: Will Universities Respond To The AI Moment?
item.author: Kevin Frazier, Juliana Schroeder, Brian Frye, Nathanael Fast, and Rob Greer
item.content:encoded: A key role universities play in society is providing knowledge that can guide public action. Moreover, public universities have a legal duty to serve the public. We expect researchers in universities to produce and disseminate knowledge that can ultimately advance human flourishing and meet the informational needs of lawmakers, civil society, and the public generally. Yet too many schools are currently failing to meet this expectation in key domains. Nearly four years after the launch of ChatGPT sparked humanity’s most pressing technological moment, many public stakeholders are left with more questions than answers about how to navigate this AI moment. Universities have only just begun to enable scholars and students to contribute to the massive task of providing adequate knowledge to guide societal action with respect to AI. This delay–perhaps forgivable for a brief period of time given that universities will never move at the speed of startups–is eroding the capacity and, as a result, legitimacy of these critical institutions. The longer that universities operate as if society were not undergoing fundamental change, the faster that faculty members will depart for other opportunities (e.g., in industry), potential and current students will opt for alternative paths to education, and stakeholders will decrease or even withhold ongoing financial support. Other individuals and more nimble organizations have rushed to fill the informational vacuum. AI labs, research institutes, and partisan entities now play a heavy role in shaping how the public and elected officials think about this moment. However, these parties–no matter how well-intentioned–have biases that may skew public discourse and lack the legitimacy of institutions like universities, which are built to shield researchers from major conflicts of interest. The exodus of talent from many universities is partially outside of their hands. Federal and state lawmakers often control the resources available to public institutions. They have yet to equip universities with the resources and tools required to assist with navigating this AI transition. In some cases, lawmakers have actively diminished support for higher education. The foreseeable result is that many professors cannot access leading AI models and many students lack AI training and literacy. These decisions have produced an academic community that is technically challenged in its ability to guide society through the myriad questions posed by AI. Public officials–to varying degrees and levels of specificity–flag for universities what studies, projects, and events would help meet public informational needs, but universities may not prioritize that work. For example, agencies sometimes issue requests for information–invitations for the public, especially individuals with relevant expertise–that do not result in meaningful engagement. At the federal level, agencies often receive fewer than ten comments on critical regulatory questions. More targeted outreach programs to scholars could provide agencies with more information as well as give academics a chance to share their perspectives. Relatedly, when legislative committees at the state level hold hearings on topics closely studied by a nearby university, they often opt to invite politically connected witnesses rather than professors. This preference may make for good politics but it leaves academics on the sidelines. A small amount of effort by these state actors could go a long way toward helping academics shift their research priorities. In this way, external actors may be partly to blame for the increasing irrelevance of higher education in AI governance conversations. But universities should also take some responsibility. Even if professors were equipped with the latest AI, some would likely fail to use it–preferring to stick to the syllabus they’ve taught from for decades and investigate the topics that they find most interesting, regardless of societal relevance. If professors persist in the belief that AI is something they can ignore and act as though they have no responsibility to monitor and contribute to the public knowledge, there’s little reason for such public funds to go toward AI tools at universities nor to improve outreach to academics to assist with AI-related questions.Academics are not passive players in decisions to cut funds and reduce support. Across disciplines, academics have maintained incentive structures that permit many scholars to act as though it’s still 2022. In response, some academics who appreciate the scale, speed, and societal significance of AI have left the Ivory Tower for the Silicon Tower, where the pay is higher, the tools are more sophisticated, and the culture rewards those who dive into the most important inquiries. Given these challenges, what can be done? This essay provides an initial call for reform, to which we hope others will also contribute. Questions of how to resolve the compensation gulf between industry and academia are left for another time. Universities–including faculty, staff, administrators, and related organizations and networks–can still make progress on establishing the conditions for increased and expedited AI research by those who opt to stay in academia. These reforms should satisfy several foundational principles, such as protecting academic freedom, creating meaningful opportunities for student participation, and addressing issues with particular importance to the university’s surrounding community. Again, this is a starting point. We invite academics and others to share this call for reform, add to it, and amend it; what we should not do is carry on as normal. Instead, we call for the vast majority of scholars to substantially re-orient their research, writing, teaching and service around AI. We think that our legislators, civil society organizations, and neighbors would be better off with too much analysis of AI, rather than too little. We’re currently living in a world with too little analysis and it’s far from satisfactory. Not every scholar should pivot to addressing AI directly, but the majority of departments should be able to point to how their collective expertise contributes to a better societal response to this moment. A surge in focus and expenditure on AI need not last forever but is highly needed at the moment.Recommendation #1: Identify and Prioritize Societally Important Research QuestionsProfessional organizations like the Association of American Law Schools (“AALS”), which represents law schools and law professors, should establish and support shared services that collect consequential questions about AI from lawmakers and AI stakeholders, such as frontier AI labs and research entities, and connect them with relevant academic communities. Staff at these organizations have extensive knowledge of the communities that exist within the discipline as well as how best to share research, advice, and engagement opportunities (as explored below). Additionally, participating universities can and should set up means to receive AI-related requests to provide yet another avenue for scholars to learn about how they can contribute. Imagine, for example, if universities designated a “legislative research liaison” who had the sole purpose of working with the legislature to specify their knowledge gaps. (It is worth noting that some universities already have government affairs teams that commonly interact with legislators, albeit not necessarily for this purpose.)Of course, individuals, organizations, and governing bodies can also share their informational needs with the Ivory Tower. This need not be a costly endeavor. For instance, state legislative committees could start their next legislative session with a hearing that culminates in a research agenda that is published and sent directly to all universities. Recommendation #2: Enable The Necessary Resources for Timely and Thorough Research on AIState and federal officials, as well as AI stakeholders seeking expedited expert analysis of complex questions, should ensure that participating scholars have the resources to offer valuable insights. As it stands, universities have far too few tokens, limited access to frontier models (sometimes because of their own outdated procurement standards and IT policies), and, in some cases, minimal understanding of the latest developments in AI (such as the existing and near-future capabilities of AI). Government officials counting on scholars to help them in their work ought to invest in their capacity to do so. AI research is not cheap. Universities are struggling to provide meaningful access to faculty, staff, and students given the high costs of many AI systems and the variability of usage-based expenses. Rather than wait for universities to procure such access, some professors are trading university roles for the lab gigs–joining labs where they know that they will be able to use the latest and greatest AI. Legislatures have yet to make the sort of sizable investments in universities required to meet the demand for AI access among experts nor to compensate experts enough to keep them on campus. In fiscal year 2025, the average state appropriation for higher education amounted to just a 2 percent increase when adjusted for inflation. AI labs likewise counting on scholars to assist with readying society for their transformative technology ought to lower barriers to academic investigation. While labs have offered some universities financial breaks on their tools and permitted some degree of support to researchers, there’s substantial room for improvement. Labs, including Google and Anthropic, are sitting on vast troves of user data that can inform everything from how AI may impact the labor market to the extent to which individuals are becoming reliant on AI tools for sensitive tasks. Universities could unleash their extensive interdisciplinary experts on such data if labs facilitated access. Labs may have justifiable reasons for holding that information close to the chest. In the wrong hands, data related to user habits, interests, and goals could lead to problematic outcomes. That said, Anthropic, OpenAI, and others cannot at once stress their concern about society’s readiness for transformative AI while keeping the information necessary to assist with that effort locked away. Recommendation #3: Reward Contributions to Societally Relevant Work on AIAcademics may be hesitant to alter their research agenda and planned publication goals if doing so is likely to block professional progress. Tenure requirements are often tied to adherence to the existing, protracted processes. What’s more, even those requirements are completed on paper–i.e. publication of a certain number of articles, tenure decisions are commonly shaped by norms and biases that further obligate applicants to invest in the status quo. For example, in the discipline of economics, tenure may be especially likely to be awarded if the applicant has published in one of five journals. Alternative contributions to the discipline, especially those done in response to demand for input on AI questions, should clearly and meaningfully inform tenure, compensation, professional recognition, and perhaps university obligations, such as committee assignments. In addition to rewarding traditional research, universities eager to meet this AI moment should formalize recognition of the following: public engagement research (albeit likely in a truncated form and via more accessible outlets),advice (testifying before legislative bodies, responding directly to government requests for information and the equivalent from labs), and engagement (meeting with legislators, regulators, and AI company policy staff, teaching community courses, serving as an expert at community forums).Accounting for these contributions to a moment of informational demand would return universities to their historical focus on knowledge creation and dissemination. Rep. Jordan Morrill, author of the eponymous act that created the nation’s land grant universities, introduced the legislation with the following vision: “Let us have such colleges as may rightfully claim the authority of teachers to announce facts, fix laws, and scatter broadcast that knowledge which will provide useful in building up a great nation.” That guiding principle informed subsequent legislation. The Hatch Act, enacted in 1887, set up “agricultural experimentation systems” at universities in each state for the purpose of:acquiring and diffusing among the people of the United States useful and practical information on subjects connected with agriculture, and to promote scientific investigation and experiment respecting the principles and application of agricultural science.These academic entities were expected to “conduct original research or verify experiments” related to timely agricultural questions and to produce “reports of progress . . . at least once in three months, one copy of which shall be sent to each newspaper in the states in which they are respectively located, and to such individuals actually engaged in farming as may request the same.” Notably, these reports were to be sent via the “mails of the United States” at no charge to the recipient.Realization of Morrill’s vision and replication (with some adaptation) of the Hatch Act’s provisions in modern times would transform modern universities, many of which have serially drifted from their respective missions. Recommendation #4: Accelerate Publication and Delivery to StakeholdersAcademic research tends to move at the speed of their respective research journals, which are rarely known for their haste. As of 2013, the publication cycle–from submission to public distribution–in business and economic journals often took 18 months; physics, comparatively moving at hyper-speed, averaged 9 months for that cycle. While some degree of delay is unquestionably necessary to probe and refine research, many scholars would conclude that the time between paper submission and publication could be shortened with minimal or, given the speed of AI, perhaps even justifiable losses to quality. Rather than tolerate continued reliance on those processes, domains should identify suitable alternatives that may allow for sufficient review while not unnecessarily delaying release. While many pre-print avenues exist, such as ArXiv and SSRN, it may nevertheless still be the case that the existing norms around length and formatting standards still slow a scholar’s dissemination of information that may be especially valuable to AI stakeholders. For example, it may be the case that in certain scenarios the most valuable thing to state or federal officials is a wide-range of white papers or even two-page memos from a range of practitioners. Such memos would substantially depart from the traditional research paper in just about every domain yet have an incredible impact on a pressing policy matter. Minimally, disciplines should commit to making their research outputs open source when possible. Academic research that lives behind a paywall will inevitably fall short of its potential to contribute to public discourse. Yet, in many disciplines only a fraction of articles are open source. Theoretically, authors of paywalled pieces may share shorter, more accessible versions through alternative means. Still, it’s antithetical to the mission of universities–especially public universities–to impose gates on knowledge. The need for open knowledge is all the greater with respect to research that addresses timely matters, such as AI. Furthermore, the materials, data, and analysis code underlying empirical research (when relevant) should be made publicly available and be as transparent as possible. By adhering to this principle of open science, empirical fields can move faster, providing opportunities to ascertain which findings are reproducible and replicable more quickly.Universities have obligations to help support the societies in which they are embedded. Novel problems and possibilities presented by this AI moment undoubtedly call for substantial assistance from our educational institutions. The call has not been answered. In fact, many of the individuals best suited to assist universities at this time of public need are leaving. The public ought to demand more–from universities, from state and federal government officials, and from AI labs. Universities can and should change their priorities and practices to better serve their external stakeholders. Different universities will adopt different approaches. Some will be more successful than others. This letter is meant to spark conversations that lead to tangible reforms,, not to advance a single best approach. Each discipline and institution may have varied answers but we think they all ought to center on a contemporary version of what Walter Murray, first president of the University of Saskatchewan, wrote in 1908: What is the sphere of the university? Its watchword is service—service of the state in the things that make for happiness and virtue as well as the things that make for wealth. No form of that service is too mean or too exalted for the university. It is as fitting for the university, through correspondence classes, extension courses, supervision of farmers’ clubs, traveling libraries, women’s institutes or musical tests to place within the reach of the solitary student, the distant townsman, the farmer in his hours of leisure or the mothers and daughters in the home the opportunities for adding to their stores of knowledge and enjoyment, as it is that the university should foster researches into the properties of radium or the causes and cure of swamp fever.It is an obligation for universities to serve the public. The need is especially high in this time of drastic technological change, with AI adoption happening faster than the adoption of any other technology in human history. We hope universities will embrace the recommendations in this essay, responding more effectively to the AI moment.

item.title: Fridge hack costing millions and sparking fires stemmed from poor security
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Earlier this week, a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction, causing spoilage of untold tons of perishables and, in some cases, fires. As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it.French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit). By the time the mass compromise was discovered, food was spoiled, and in some cases their electrical systems caught fire.The hacks that didn't have to happenMultiple security advisories and public research reports show that all three of the controller models reportedly hacked in the incident—sold by Danfoss of Denmark and Dixell and its parent company Copeland in the US—contained critical vulnerabilities that allow attackers to remotely log in to the devices with the same system rights as administrators. Until recently, Danfoss controllers, for instance, used a credential that changes each day. The password is generated by the publicly available firmware based on the date. A hacker who takes the time to analyze the code can do the same thing on any device that hasn’t received a recent update. Daily passwords are identical across models located in hundreds or thousands of stores.

item.title: ICE’s Lies About A Man Officer Ran Over Undone By Footage Captured By Nearby CCTV Camera
item.author: Tim Cushing
item.content:encoded: ICE alleged in a statement that “Parra-Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”ABC13 reached out to an ICE spokesperson, who said agents were attempting to arrest Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who was their intended target.ICE alleges Mendoza-Cervantes entered the United States illegally from Mexico five times and had a final order of removal issued by a judge. The agency also alleges Parra-Hernandez is in the country illegally.Now, if you’re an absolute prick (or an ICE officer, but I repeat myself), you may think this lie is correct. After all, Miguel Parra-Hernandez struck by the of an ICE vehicle while through a parking lot. So, he was in of an ICE vehicle when things happened that ICE attributes to (“was struck”). But the verbal tense means everything here. If all you saw or heard was the ICE statement, you would assume the man carelessly crossed a street or inadvertently stepped out into the path of an already-moving ICE vehicle. But the proper tense here is “running” and he wasn’t initially running “in front” of an ICE vehicle. The ICE vehicle (and its unnamed driver) had to cross a street and cut through a parking lot to… um… “was struck” Parra-Hernandez. The rest of the statement is the usual ICE bullshit meant to fool idiots into believing whatever happens to migrants is their own fault, as though being in the country illegally should be met with something that looks a lot like attempted vehicular manslaughter. That the person ICE officers ran over wasn’t even the (purported) target of this arrest attempt makes this statement even stupider than it already is. If you choose to believe ICE rather than me, feel free to watch the recording yourself. And then smack yourself around a bit for being exactly the rube this administration assumes everyone — even its voting base — to be. What you’ll see here is Parra-Hernandez exiting a truck stopped on the street and running through a parking lot. Shortly thereafter, you’ll see the ICE vehicle accelerate from across the street and aim the accelerating vehicle directly at the running person as it enters the parking lot. While you won’t actually see the impact (due to another vehicle in the lot that seems to be part of the ICE posse), the end result was an ICE officer running over a fleeing person. And how it happens looks very deliberate. Even if you give ICE a benefit of doubt it certainly hasn’t earned, the best case scenario is that the driver thought he could safely do some sort of pedestrian PIT maneuver or realized far too late that they wouldn’t be able to slow down in time. But don’t bounce out the video quite yet. There’s more! An ICE officer enters the abandoned truck and parks it in the parking lot in a spot where it could easily be believed that a fleeing person would have “inadvertently” crossed paths with an ICE pursuit vehicle. While some might speculate that ICE needed to remove the abandoned vehicle from the nearby street for public safety or whatever, the fact that it was conspicuously parked where it could shore up ICE’s narrative undercuts any assumptions of innocence on ICE’s part.Furthermore, the vehicle was now part of an active crime scene, which meant ICE should never have moved it at all. Running someone over with a car is a crime, even if it’s accidental. An investigation needed to happen, but ICE compromised the crime scene when it absolutely didn’t need to, even if its intentions (allow traffic to flow) were pure. There were plenty of ICE officers on the scene that could have directed traffic until the locals showed up.Given all of that, it’s 100% safe to assume the only reason the vehicle was moved was to put the truck in the path of the ICE vehicle after the fact, thus making its “ran out in front of our vehicle” narrative a bit more believable. While there is now an independent investigation underway, it’s unlikely ICE will cooperate in any way. And it’s probably only a matter of time before the feds step in and sweep this under a rug that cannot possibly have any more room for additional cover-ups. At least the local prosecutor and sheriff’s office seem interested in digging into this, rather than just run interference for Trump’s anti-migrant efforts. On Saturday, Harris County Attorney Abbie Kamin issued a statement regarding the incident, stating in part:“Time is of the essence in getting the facts, and the public deserves clear, accurate answers.ICE must cooperate fully with the local investigation. My office supports Sheriff Ed Gonzalez and District Attorney Sean Teare in their ongoing independent investigation, and the Harris County Attorney’s Office stands ready to assist and support these critical efforts. We will continue to monitor developments closely as the facts become clear.Let’s raise a glass to the undertrained, overly aggressive officers of ICE. They can’t get away with much because they’re too stupid and aggro to realize there are cameras everywhere these days. And even if they can’t be bothered to wear/activate the mandated body cams ICE has been dragging its feet about since late last year, someone or something else is bound to catch them in the act. But until we get a few convictions nailed down, the entire administration will remain the embodiment of Trump’s “I could shoot someone on Fifth Ave. and get away with it” (lightly paraphrased, you MAGA pedants) boast.

item.title: US Tech Giants Warn Europe That Data Sovereignty Requirements Could Cost $128 Billion
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
A study commissioned by CCIA Europe, whose members include Amazon, Google, and Meta, estimates that the EU's proposed Cloud and AI Development Act could impose 115 billion euros ($128 billion) in costs over a decade as governments and companies migrate workloads and rewrite software. The figure is more than six times the European Commission's upper estimate. However, roughly 80 billion euros ($89 billion) of it comes from a modeled scenario assuming sovereignty rules are extended to 25% of cloud workloads in essential private-sector industries.The Register reports: The report specifically targets Article 31 of the proposed legislation, which it says could allow the Commission to extend sovereignty requirements into essential private-sector services. CCIA argues that forcing businesses to move away from existing cloud infrastructure could trigger expensive software redevelopment projects, with code rewriting and re-architecting accounting for 69 percent of its estimated costs.
Luxembourg would apparently take the biggest hit, with the study putting the cost at 1,711 euros per worker over ten years. Denmark (905 euros), Austria (900 euros), and Finland (864 euros) also face hefty bills, as does Ireland (856 euros), which hosts the European headquarters of several US tech giants. CCIA is urging EU governments to overhaul the proposed legislation, limit sovereignty restrictions to sensitive workloads, and abandon requirements based on corporate origin or personnel nationality in favor of what it calls risk-based technical safeguards.
"Member States cannot rely on the Commission's incomplete estimates when deciding CADA's strict sovereignty requirements for cloud and AI providers," said Mitchell Rutledge, CCIA Europe's policy manager. "Taxpayers and businesses will foot the bill, yet the official assessment missed 70 percent of CADA's true impact." For AWS and Google, offering European customers greater control over their data also helps retain business that might otherwise migrate to European competitors. It's a rather convenient arrangement: sell customers sovereignty on one hand, while an industry association representing your interests warns governments against imposing too much of it on the other.

item.title: Google Is Silently Linking Your Phone Number Across All Signed-In Accounts

Android Authority reports: As spotted in a recent Reddit thread, users report receiving confirmation emails out of the blue from "noreply-phone-verification@google.com" stating that their phone number has been verified. The feature, known in Google settings as "Phone number verification," links your active phone number across all Google accounts signed in on the same phone, including secondary profiles, work accounts, and throwaway handles.
Google's support documentation has long noted that it periodically re-verifies your device's phone number to keep communication and recovery features up to date. However, this support page was updated sometime between August and October 2025 to add this rather aggressive behavior of turning on phone number verification by default, as well as adding all phone numbers to all Google accounts signed in on the device. To disable automatic phone number verification on Android, open your phone's Settings app, tap Google, and select the All Services tab. Under Privacy & Security, find Phone number verification and turn off Verify phone numbers automatically.
"[T]urning off the phone number verification toggle only prevents future linking," notes the report. "If Google has already attached your number across secondary accounts, you will need to open your Google Account Personal Info page, head to Contact info > Phone, and manually remove the number from each profile where it doesn't belong."

item.title: MAGA Built The Censorship Machine It Spent Years Falsely Accusing Democrats Of Building
item.author: Mike Masnick
item.content:encoded: This is not a unique or new observation, but so many MAGA attacks on others are projection, claiming that Democrats were doing the very things that MAGA always knew they would do if they were in charge. We’ve certainly spent plenty of time talking about Donald Trump’s myriad and non-stopattacks on free speech, and just recently I wrote about how Trump has turned his FCC into the very “ministry of truth” that Fox News falsely claimed Biden had created. But two recent articles show how MAGA has gone all in on doing the two things it most loudly (and falsely) accused the other side of: suppressing free speech on campus, and running a “censorship industrial complex” to coerce private companies into silencing speech it doesn’t like.At Texas Tech, medical students no longer learn about racial disparities in medical care. Faculty at the university’s medical center in Lubbock were advised to “refrain from treating transgender patients, for any medical condition, if a medical student was present,”filed by the American Association of University Professors. (When asked for comment, a spokesperson said that the university’s “written guidance is publicly available and expressly protects instruction necessary for licensure and patient care.”) According to the same lawsuit, the censorship bot—officially known as the Course Content Review Process—ordered a Tech philosophy professor to remove Plato’s Republic from a syllabus because “it references Plato’s beliefs concerning gender roles and homosexuality.”Professors in the Texas A&M system have had to strip their syllabi too. According, last January, Aaron George, a professor at Tarleton State University, was told by administrators to remove A Gay Manifesto, a Stonewall-era LGBTQ-rights pamphlet, and White Flight, a history of urban segregation, from his American-political-history course. After a student complained that a different class the professor taught violated university policy, George was informed by administrators that it would be canceled if he did not make “necessary” (but unspecified) changes. He cut a reference in the course description to the significance of the Fourteenth Amendment for LGBTQ rights, and the class was allowed to proceed.The University of Texas at Austin, the flagship school of the UT system, announced last month that it was eliminating majors in Africana studies, Mexican American and Latino studies, women’s and gender studies, and race and migration studies. More than 100 courses have been flagged for removal from the core curriculum, primarily ones relating to slavery, race, gender, sexuality, and the environment. Consolidating majors isn’t necessarily nefarious, nor is rethinking a core curriculum (a central group of courses from which students must take a certain number to graduate). But these changes are happening, Lauren Gutterman, an American studies professor at UT, told me, “entirely because of the political context.”Where are all the folks who spent years screaming about “academic freedom” and insisting that colleges were censoring conservative speech? Remember how Bari Weiss and Joe Lonsdale created their “University of Austin” because (they falsely claimed) there were no universities where people could speak freely — and then they fired someone for suggesting that there might be some value in thinking about the importance of diversity.Hilariously, Texas Governor Greg Abbott had signed a bill back in 2019 guaranteeing “free speech on campus.” But as Serwer’s piece details, these days there are all sorts of banned topics on Texas college campuses, and basically none of free speech grifters who spent years crying crocodile tears over supposed attacks on “campus speech” seem to have anything to say about it.Even more ridiculous, Serwer details how Texas Tech is using AI to scan syllabi for wrongthink, with predictably stupid results:Alan Barenberg, a history professor who specializes in the Soviet Union, was told to remove readings by the Princeton historian Joan Scott and the French philosopher Michel Foucault from his Ph.D.-level historiography class, after they were flagged by the AI—whose assessments he described to me as “completely inaccurate.” It also seemed to have mixed his course up with a different one. The texts were part of a unit of the class related to how treatment of gender in historical research has changed over time. “These things have been taught in classes for a long time,” Barenberg told me. The material is controversial, he said, only “in the eyes of a few people who aren’t even actually on campus.”“The fact that the system AI doesn’t work, that it makes inaccurate pronouncements—that’s a feature, not a bug. They don’t care if it’s accurate or not. They just want to be able to say, Look, we’re making sure that your children are not being exposed to these horrible ideas from these radical professors,” Barenberg said. “A key part of how authoritarian systems often work is that, through the vagueness and sending up signals and vibes, they’re essentially saying, You know what not to do, but being deliberately vague about it.”Although the AI is now reviewing only some courses, the university could extend the process to more. For now, professors are the ones responsible for volunteering whether their own materials may be considered controversial. Many, unsure of what might trigger the bot, told me that they had private conversations with administrators who told them to simply self-censor and remove materials from their courses in advance, so as not to draw the wrath of leadership or lawmakers.So the “free speech on campus” crowd is now actively censoring speech on campus because a computer program told them it was woke. What could go wrong?You can follow the links there to get more details, but the most important detail is that when some individuals and two MAGA-run states sued the Biden admin over the supposed “censorship industrial complex,” it was two Trump-appointed Supreme Court Justices — Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — who pointed out how wrong they were.During oral arguments Kavanaugh practically laughed at the lawyer making these claims, pointing out that government officials merely pressing their side of the story with no associated threats or coercion happens every damn day in the government, and is not even remotely close to censorship. Then Coney Barrett wrote the decision of the court, noting the complete lack of evidence tying any government outreach to actual moderation decisions, and called the lower court judge’s factual findings “clearly erroneous.” That resulted in the case being sent back for lack of standing due to the fact that there was zero evidence presented of any coercive behavior.So there was no Biden “censorship industrial complex,” but there absolutely is a Trump one. As Fisher notes:And not a peep from those who falsely argued that it existed under Biden. How strange.Once again, those complaints were all lies and projection. Richard Hanania, the far right commentator who spent years spreading hate and white supremacy online and now pretends to have turned against the very MAGA Trumpism he long supported, at least admitted clearly, back before Elon Musk took over Twitter, that right wingers like himself only scream about “censorship” because they want to do it themselves. This was in response to him getting banned from (again, pre-Elon) Twitter for violating its rules against hateful conduct. At the time, he said:I don’t feel particularly oppressed by leftists. They give me a lot more free speech than I would give them if the tables were turned. If I owned Twitter, I wouldn’t let feminists, trans activists, or socialists post. Why should I? They’re wrong about everything and bad for society. Twitter is a company that is overwhelmingly liberal, and I’m actually impressed they let me get away with the things I’ve been saying for this long.But that kind of honesty about how much MAGA authoritarians want to censor people while screaming about non-existent “censorship” from the other side is rare.Still, it would be nice if everyone stopped pretending that Greg Abbott, Donald Trump, or Elon Musk ever stood for free speech at all. They all whined about free speech solely as a means to make sure that they were in charge of censoring those they disliked.

item.title: Anthropic Warns Small AI Models Could Self-Replicate Through IoT Devices
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that's capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results do raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms.
Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that "a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there's no centralized point to shut off -- though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own." Smaller AI models require much less powerful hardware to run than do frontier models. Anthropic ran small open-weight models on real or simulated low-cost, off-brand Android TV boxes and other types of IoT hardware. Company researchers found that by using quantization to represent the models using fewer bits and splitting the workloads into "shards" running on each device, the models were able to establish inference, meaning that the model weights loaded and could generate output.
[...] This finding was the starting point for further research that asked: Would it be possible for small models to create self-replicating infections that run themselves on IoT devices the way traditional IoT worms, like Mirai, install DDoS code and other payloads? Unlike Mirai, these AI worms could pose a much higher threat, since the models could tailor exploits and payloads dynamically, depending on the target. Once such an infection chain began, it might also be harder for defenders to stop it. "Such an 'AI worm' could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware," Anthropic said. "Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload." Further reading: Anthropic Bans Cruelty Toward Claude

item.title: Court Filings Show DHS Is Collecting Info On Protesters, Feeding It To Palantir
item.author: Tim Cushing
item.content:encoded: More evidence is piling up that contradicts the almost-but-not-quite denials given by administration officials in response to allegations about the DHS compiling a database to keep tabs on protesters. Just a few months ago, “Immigration Czar” Todd Lyons was trying to turn credible accusations into a nothingburger by deploying a few vague and trite statements that didn’t actually add up to real denial. Protesters were reporting that immigration officers were taking photos of protesters, trying to gather other identifying info from them when accosting them, and then doing truly nasty stuff plainly meant to deter them from engaging in further protests or simply trying to document what ICE officers were doing out in the field. Protesters and observers who have encountered ICE officers have reported multiple drive-bys by ICE officers at their personal homes, calls from unidentified officers containing veiled threats of punishment, and other forms of intimidation that are reliant on having enough collected data to locate people’s homes, phone numbers, places of business, etc. Rep. Lou Correa, D-Calif., cited a well-circulated clip of an ICE agent in Portland, Maine, telling a person videotaping that she would be added to a “nice little database.” “I can’t speak for that individual,” said Todd Lyons, who serves as acting director of ICE. “But I can assure you that there is no database that’s tracking United States citizens.”Lyons doubled down on his denials about the database’s existence during a Senate hearing Thursday. When asked if ICE is giving protester information to any other agency, Lyons said: “We do not.” In his official response to congressional oversight, Lyons went a bit further… which only made things worse.If individuals who interact with ICE officers are not arrested or detained, any information collected during those encounters is maintained consistent with applicable law and DHS and ICE policies and is treated as an official government record.That’s the information-gathering side of things, which clearly states that ICE collecting information on more than just the people it arrests. And since it’s collecting this information on non-arrestees in the normal course of business, the compilation is undeniably happening. Whether or not this information is segregated from the rest of the stuff ICE gathers is hardly consequential, which makes this statement from Lyons especially meaningless.DHS is not creating or maintaining a separate, standalone database for individuals encountered that haven’t been arrested or detained.You don’t have to create a database. You don’t even have to silo it off. You can just dump this info in with the rest of the stuff and let those with access use this info to track down protesters in order to intimidate them. A recent court filing in a lawsuit against the DHS brought by anti-ICE protesters in Maine (one that alleges a lot of truly troubling behavior by ICE officers) says ICE is shoving this info into Palantir’s gaping data maw, presumably to expedite future threats, intimidation, and retaliation against First Amendment-protected activity.An explosive and newly partially unsealed court filing alleges that the US Department of Homeland Security built up dossiers on ICE observers—including their photos, license plate numbers, and other information—and stored them in a system called the Investigative Case Management database, which was built by Palantir.Plaintiffs allege in the filing, which is heavily based on documents produced by the government and depositions of DHS agents, that agents had a practice of intimidating protesters and observers. They did this, the filing says, by doing drive-bys of the observers’ homes and, in the case of at least one observer, requiring that she be referred to secondary inspection any time she tries to cross the border until at least January 2027.The allegations are only going to get more serious the further this case proceeds. The plaintiffs are still operating with limited information, but what little they have already suggests ICE officers routinely engage in retaliatory acts against protesters and observers. From the filing [PDF]:While the case is still in its preliminary stage, with only limited discovery, the record demonstrates that agents routinely collect images of observers’ faces and license plates, and have created retaliatory investigative records about their protected activity. Agents also threatened multiple observers with being placed on watchlists, and have continued their practice of intimidating drive-bys: in June of this year, an agent led Plaintiff Hilton to the address on her driver’s license and conspicuously stopped in front of the house. Other Mainers have experienced the same. All Plaintiffs have experienced concrete harm and have been chilled in the exercise of their First Amendment rights: Williams and Pantos have stopped all observation activity entirely, and Hilton and Fagan have reduced their protected activity or taken other precautions while doing so.Whatever guidelines ICE may have in place (if any) to prevent ICE officers from gathering info on protesters and observers clearly isn’t working. The filing mentions multiple times where ICE officers have directly told the people they’re accosting that they would be adding them to the ICM (ICE’s case management system) or, worse, a “domestic terrorism watchlist.” These are credible allegations, especially since some of these threats from officers have been recorded. The plaintiff who’s allegedly now facing mandatory secondary inspection at all border crossings for the next six months lends a lot of credence to claims about being added to terrorism watchlists.DHS’s denial is hardly worth noting. A spokesperson for DHS calls the case “meritless” and says that “the underlying lawsuit is based on the lie that there is a database of ‘domestic terrorists’ run by DHS.”All this says is that the DHS doesn’t “run” the “domestic terrorists” database. While that is true (the Terrorist Screening Dataset is overseen by the DOJ and “run” by the FBI), the Terrorist Screening Center is a multi-agency operation (including the DHS and its components) that “manages” (direct quote here) its operations. Furthermore, the DHS and its components are designated “nominators,” which means exactly what’s being denied by DHS spokespeople: officers do have the power to put people on “terrorist watchlists.” Whether or not this lawsuit leads to more discovery, there’s no reason to give the DHS the benefit of a doubt while waiting for more information to roll in. It has already shown it’s willing to violate rights, ignore court orders, and pretend existing immigration laws don’t actually say what they say. The mass deportation machinery deployed by the Trump administration is in a state of constant acceleration. Anything that might reduce a bit of the friction — even if it’s clearly unconstitutional acts of intimidation — will be deployed until a court tells it to stop… and then for awhile after that, if recent history is any indication. And it’s all being aided by a company that’s collecting tens of millions of dollars to, basically, help ICE agents connect these dots faster.

item.title: There’s Nothing Mysterious or Unusual About the Viral German Sexual Harassment Robot
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: Let’s briefly deconstruct a viral or soon to be viral story out of Cologne, Germany regarding an incident in which a “remotely controlled robot grabs 16-year-old's buttocks” and “performed thrusting movements against her,” .I have begun to see this story percolate around the English-speaking internet because it is absurd and not good, and has already been aggregated to hell by social media meme pages with essentially zero information other than this absurd police image: The Cologne Police did not exactly help matters by issuing a short press release that treats the robot as mysterious, the circumstances as mysterious, and the evidence as “unusual.” The Cologne Police’s Facebook post featuring a photo of the mustachioed robot reads “A red-gold robot triggered a police operation on the Cologne Ring on Sunday night (October 11). The device is said to have touched a 16-year-old girl's buttocks and performed thrusting movements against her […] The police are now investigating how the robot worked at the time of the assault and whether someone was deliberately controlling its movements. Emergency services seized the robot and two mobile phones from the suspect. The police are investigating on suspicion of defamation on a sexual basis.”Coverage by even well-resourced outlets like CNN, CBC, and the BBC have almost no information beyond the police press release, which is lazy and stupid, because it is possible to figure out everything that happened here with three seconds of clicking around the internet. The Associated Press wrote that the entire phenomenon is "new territory" for the police, which, I'm sorry to say, men using tech to harass women on livestreams in 2026 is not "unusual" or "new territory" and hasn't been for many years. The English coverage of the incident looks like this:In fact, with a small amount of Googling and/or clicking around social media, it is easy to find out everything you would ever need to know about the robot and what happened here. The tl;dr is that a 16-year-old German Twitch IRL livestreamer named Agaamuza has been streaming himself using an off-the-shelf $5,000 robot from a company named Unitree to walk around Cologne and bother people outside of bars in the way that extremely annoying Twitch livestreamers and TikTok stars have been doing for years. In a recent livestream, Agaamuza or one of his friends uses the robot to grab a girl’s ass, the boys laugh about it, and the police get involved. Twitch has temporarily suspended his channel from streaming but because of the social media clipping economy, there are zillions of videos of the streamers and the robot percolating across Instagram, YouTube, and TikTok. On the actual internet where real people click around and don't regurgitate police statements and pretend they're reporting the news, you can see the entire arc of what happened, which now includes an hour-long "statement" Twitch video in which Agaamuza streams with the robot dressed in striped prison clothes.The slightly longer version: For at least a few weeks, Agaamuza and his friends put a mustache and giant chain necklace on the robot, call him “Ahmad the Robot,” and film people’s reactions to the robot thrusting, dancing, punching the sky, walking into stores, etc. Most of these videos are annoying but not illegal. They are very much a part of YouTube / Twitch “prank” culture, in which men—almost always men—film themselves hitting on women, interviewing people outside of bars, and doing stupid shit in public. Agaamuza and “Ahmad the Robot” have become minor characters in the German Twitch streaming world over the last few weeks. The robot in question is the Unitree R1, which costs between $4,900 and $5,900 depending on the specific model. Unitree is a Chinese robot company that makes the R1 and a robot dog that has become vaguely popular among people who are excited about humanoid robots and gadget YouTubers. Unitree is kind of a Boston Dynamics-esque company in that it makes lots of YouTube videos of its robots doing cartwheels and backflips and fighting other robots, and regularly goes viral for it. The capabilities of the R1 robot are not a secret and can be found in any number of YouTube videos or on Unitree’s website (which is to say that the R1 is not a mysterious harassment or spy robot as it has been portrayed in some of the aggregations of this story I’ve seen). Anyways, over the weekend while live-streaming, Agaamuza or one of his friends has the robot walk into a group of girls standing on the street in Cologne. “Oh my god oh my god Ahmad,” one of the streamers says, as they walk the robot directly into a girl’s ass. One of the girls says “Oh my god stop.” The boys say “Hey, he wants to meet you, do you want to meet him?” The girls say no. The robot begins thrusting its arms in the air (the girls have moved away at this point), and the streamers start screaming “no brother, no bro oh man.” The girls tell the streamers to leave them alone and then walk away. In his statement video, Agaamuza says that the robot simply ran into the girl and didn't grope her. The robot certainly did run into her, the whole thing was harassing and annoying; in the United States, these sorts of things happen on Twitch constantly, generally with no consequences.What happened is bad, and is not much different than the types of clips of men harassing women that go viral all the time on social media, many of them filmed or streamed surreptitiously using Meta’s AI glasses. What actually is unusual about this case is that the police appear to actually be taking it seriously.

item.title: Dutch Tax Authorities Cancel Microsoft 365 Cloud Rollout, Turn Toward Open Source
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from ZDNet: The Netherlands' Tax and Customs Administration has abandoned its planned Microsoft 365 public-cloud rollout. Why? The reasons were clear at the Open Source Summit Europe conference, where the Linux Foundation (LF) released the 2026 State of Open Source in Europe. In it, the nonprofit, pro-open-source organization revealed that 94% of European Union (EU) organizations say digital sovereignty is important, with 61% considering it very important. As Thierry Carrez, the Linux Foundation Europe GM, said in his keynote, "Europe has clearly heard the message on digital sovereignty."
In an interview onstage at the summit, Nithya Ruff, chair of the LF board, added that it's not just Europe: "Digital sovereignty is a need that the entire world feels, whether it's Sierra Leone or the US or China." It's not just the Dutch tax collectors, though. The Netherlands is also exploring switching from Windows and proprietary software to Linux and open-source programs across the board. [...] The Netherlands had planned to switch to Microsoft 365 in 2025. The idea then was to complete the rollout by the end of 2026. About 5,000 employees had already migrated when the Dutch Advisory Council on ICT Assessment recommended reversing the public-cloud rollout in June. The government paused the plan in July; the latest announcement replaces that rollout with an on-premises/open-source approach.
The Tax and Customs Administration isn't replacing all of Microsoft Office with a single open-source suite, at least not yet. Instead, the government will keep the existing Microsoft software for now. Looking ahead, State Secretary for Finance Eelco Eerenberg set out the replacement timetable in a letter to Parliament: "In 2027, the provision for mail and calendar will be realized on-premises. Later in 2027 and 2028, European open-source solutions for personal storage and collaboration will follow. This allows us to work toward a sustainable and more autonomous solution for these functionalities." [...] For now, the on-premises email/calendar environment will still use Microsoft software, including Outlook. The open-source portion concerns personal storage and collaboration, not a wholesale replacement of Word, Excel, PowerPoint, or the entire desktop environment. As for why the Netherlands pulled back, the ICT assessment found serious concerns over "information security, information processing and future-proofing." Key issues included routing confidential documents through American servers, relying on standard Microsoft encryption rather than Double Key Encryption, and inadequate end-to-end encryption for Teams calls. The assessment also identified "vendor lock-in, reduced flexibility, concerns about digital sovereignty, and the absence of an adequate exit strategy" as dealbreakers.
ZDNet notes that other Dutch government agencies are developing an open-source alternative called DAWO (Digital Autonomous Work Environment for Government), which would begin by replacing Windows with the Linux distribution NixOS.

item.title: China Still Has Easy Access To TikTok Despite Trump ‘Fixes’
item.author: Karl Bode
item.content:encoded: Remember how the Trump administration — and folks like Brendan Carr — spent four straight years fear-mongering about China’s purported control over TikTok and its owner, ByteDance? And remember how the Trump administration (with incompetent Democratic lawmaker help) “fixed” the problem by offloading Tiktok to Trump’s billionaire buddies while still maintaining co-ownership with the Chinese?It was basically a five-year xenophobic fear campaign designed to steal the revenues of a top short-form video company that U.S. giants like Meta were struggling to compete with. And it was propped up by endless empty lip service to propaganda, consumer privacy, and national security; in turn propped up by a tech press that struggled to explain how silly and corruption-fueled it all was. After the Trump deal, U.S. operations of TikTok now had three “managing investors” that collectively owned 45 percent of the company: Oracle Corporation (Larry Ellison), Silver Lake, and MGX. Another 5 percent is owned by other new investors, 30.1 percent is “held by affiliates of certain existing investors of ByteDance; and 20 percent was retained by ByteDance.The Trump administration offloaded most of TikTok’s infrastructure to Oracle — a company with a long list of privacy violations — so they could pretend they “fixed privacy issues” with the app. They also set up a bunch of “safeguards” designed to pretend they’d cut off Chinese influence, without actually doing so. “Employees at the new company, officially named TikTok USDS Joint Venture, still work regularly with the global TikTok organization, according to current and former employees, who were granted anonymity to speak candidly, and internal communications reviewed by POLITICO Magazine. That includes coordinating over new features, sharing information about dangerous trends on the app and collaborating over policies. U.S. employees also still use an internal chat system called Lark, which was built by TikTok’s former Beijing-based parent company, ByteDance, to communicate and share information with both their U.S. and global counterparts.”Great stuff. There are other instances of largely performative attempts to keep Chinese and U.S. TikTok employees separated, but there’s no real indication this is working or being overseen by anybody competent in the U.S. government:“At TikTok office buildings, U.S. employees can go to TikTok global offices on different floors but are required to get a chaperone, an employee said, and are prohibited from bringing laptops. Prior to the deal, U.S. employees could mostly move freely between the U.S. and global offices.”It’s equally murky as to whether “the algorithm” (a subject of endless debate during the fearmongering campaign) is still maintained and updated by ByteDance engineers.Again, there’s no real indication that this was ever about anything but Trump and his allies hijacking the revenues of a profitable short-form video company under the pretense of national security. You could also easily argue that under Byetance ownership the company was at least incentivized to behave to remain in the U.S.; guys like Larry Ellison — with a long history of ethical and privacy “lapses” — really has no worries that the government will ever hold him accountable for much of anything. As we noted early on, the Chinese really don’t need TikTok to spy on Americans or funnel propaganda to the electorate. Because we’re too corrupt to regulate data brokers or pass a privacy law, most U.S. consumer data is openly accessible via the public market to anybody — including Chinese intelligence. The Trump administration is still facing a lawsuit alleging the deal is illegal. And Democrats continue to look positively feckless and ignorant for helping the Trump administration hijack an app (popular with young voters) during a presidential election season where the youth vote mattered more than ever.

item.title: Anthropic Reinvents Source Control As Claude Floods the World With Code
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic says Claude-generated code has scaled so quickly that its existing Git-based infrastructure could not keep up. In response, the company built a custom centralized source-control system called Scion, along with AI-assisted review and search tools. The Register reports: "In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day," the biz said in a blog post on Tuesday. "We don't expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce."
After several months of model prompting and five months of migration, the result is a homemade version control system called Scion, a monorepo scheme that sounds a bit like Subversion, Apache's centralized version control system. [...] Scion has been designed to meet the needs of AI agents, so the client leaves much of the work to the server; the source control queries are exposed via API so internal tools can respond without needing a local repo, and there's less synchronization but more need for server speed.
"In Scion, the unit of work is a 'changeset,' an entry in a write-ahead log," Anthropic explains. "A changeset stores most of what you'd expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent, along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage." [...] Anthropic says its bespoke system isn't right for general use. There will be no open source release. Nonetheless, the company contends that its own code scaling problems will become commonplace in other organizations over the next few months, so it wanted to share its approach -- having ample funding to pay for writing custom infrastructure tools.

item.title: In 1991, Federal Panel Blasts Vaccine Unavailability That Led To A Measles Epidemic
item.author: Timothy Geigner
item.content:encoded: The apocryphal quote supposedly from Mark Twain is one of my favorites: “History does not repeat, but it does often rhyme.” Now, there is no evidence that Twain ever actually authored these words, but it’s incredible how true they tend to be regardless. And when it comes to the current measles outbreak that is ravaging the country, and the Northeast in particular, they seem incredibly apropos. We’re suffering this outbreak for many reasons: the anti-vaxxer agenda being rendered directly into the federal government, the distrust in medical professionals and science that has been purposefully fostered by bad actors, and a general apathy for vaccinations. But if you want to know why it’s gotten worse and not better, the answer to is singular: inaction by the federal government. And if you go back to 1991, the last time the country suffered a measles epidemic this significant, you can read news stories that don’t exactly mirror our current situation, but they do rhyme. A breakdown in the vaccination system caused the nation’s worst measles epidemic in decades, and more epidemics may occur unless the system is changed, a Federal advisory panel said today.The panel, the National Vaccine Advisory Committee, said in a report, “The principal cause for the epidemic is failure to deliver vaccine to vulnerable preschool children on schedule.” It said the health care system created “barriers to obtaining immunization and fails to take advantage of many opportunities to provide vaccines to children.”It’s a similar story today, of course. Though, unlike today, I don’t have any reason to believe that governmental failures in 1991 that led to the measles epidemic at the time were purposeful. In fact, federal officials at the time responded to this report by lambasting state officials with conspiracy theories and political attacks, but by acknowledging the report’s accuracy and promising to do better. There’s no indication that the federal government at the time attempted to hide cases and deaths from measles, unlike the current administration under RFK Jr.No, this was federal advisors and federal officials working off the same set of facts and combining their efforts to make things . And better things actually got. This was, by the way, a time when the Executive Branch was also Republican. Dr. Bart, director of the National Vaccine Program Office of the Department of Health and Human Services, said the Bush Administration had been waiting for the report and would quickly plan to follow as many of the panel’s recommendations as possible.“We have a huge increases and deaths due to measles for the first time in two decades,” he said. “We also think there is some acute deterioration of the health care system, and we fear that this may be a warning flag for other problems to come.”Dr. Henderson said that immunization “is the simplest procedure in the entire medical armamentarium, and is by far the most cost effective of all the medical interventions we have.” If we cannot provide the simplest and most cost effective thing we have, he said, “what does that say about our health system? It is clear that we have a problem.”Well, then at present we have a problem. A bigger one, actually. The story at present isn’t one of government bureaucracy failing simply because big governmental systems are slow and lethargic generally. In this case, the causes of vaccine hesitancy and under-vaccination . It’s what the leadership of our health agencies are striving for. There is no argument otherwise. Kennedy has said the government is doing a great job on the measles question, even as thousands are infected and people are dying. We’ll get into this more separately, but Kennedy also has, in the middle of this outbreak, created a federal program to financially incentivize the reporting of vaccine injuries. If disease is the enemy of Americans, then Kennedy is a traitor. He’s giving aid and comfort to that enemy, plain and simple. It’s why the measles outbreak is getting worse, not better. It’s why other health conditions are on the rise, such as pertussis and mumps. What is happening right now is insane. What makes it more insane is that the lessons we learned from the last time we engaged with this enemy are barely 35 years old. Universe willing, November will pave the way for Congress to actually do something about it all.

GamesBeat reports that Rockstar plans to release Grand Theft Auto VI on PC in the first quarter of 2027, just a few months after its November 19, 2026 launch on consoles. The user base of Grand Theft Auto V skews largely towards console players, with PC players representing a small minority. With GTA VI's production budget rumored to exceed $2 billion, Rockstar is highly incentivized to pull all the levers it can as fast as it can to monetize the game's upcoming sequel -- and PC players represent a significant expansion of the GTA VI audience.
The potential benefits of launching GTA VI relatively quickly on PC go beyond the opportunity to grow the game's casual player base. Rockstar has signaled its plans to implement user-generated content creation tools into GTA VI, and the company's August 2023 acquisition of Cfx.re, the development team behind the prominent Grand Theft Auto V roleplaying server company FiveM, made it clear that Rockstar considers online roleplaying in GTA to be a factor in the game's future.
