item.title: The Metric Is Not The Mission: The End Of The Universal Internet
item.author: Konstantinos Komaitis
item.content:encoded: The Metric Is Not the Mission is a ten-part examination of how Big Tech moved from building and expanding the open internet to increasingly shaping it around its own metrics, incentives and assumptions. Across the series, the argument follows the evolution of the platform economy—from the optimism of the early internet to the growing tensions around power, prediction, geopolitics, accountability and the future of digital life.The series will be published in two parts each week over five weeks, with each installment building on the one before it. At the end of the series, the complete essay will be brought together in a single PDF edition, providing the full argument in one place.The End of the Universal InternetPart VI examined the limits of what platforms can know about us. This part widens the lens again, looking at what happens when the supposedly universal internet collides with geopolitics, national interests and the return of sovereignty.Every age constructs its own myths. The Industrial Revolution gave us the myth of endless progress: the conviction that scientific discovery and economic growth would move steadily, almost mechanically, towards a more prosperous future. The twentieth century inherited the myth of globalization, imagining that the increasing movement of goods, capital, and people would gradually soften political boundaries and render old rivalries economically irrational. The internet age produced its own variation on the same theme. Technology, we were told, would become the first truly global language. Networks would succeed where diplomacy often failed. Code would travel more easily than ideology. Connectivity would create constituencies for cooperation that governments could neither manufacture nor easily disrupt.Silicon Valley became the principal narrator of that story. Its ambitions were never presented as merely commercial. They were civilizational. Google did not simply index websites; it sought to organize the world’s information. Facebook did not describe itself as a social network so much as an instrument for making the world “more open and connected.” The rhetoric mattered because it invited users to think of these companies not as corporations competing for market share but as custodians of a new global infrastructure. They increasingly resembled institutions whose legitimacy derived from serving humanity rather than shareholders alone. And, for a remarkably long time, much of the world accepted that proposition.The claim was not entirely unreasonable. The internet had always been unusual in the way it blurred geography. An email ignored borders. A website became available almost everywhere simultaneously. Engineers from countries with profoundly different political systems collaborated through common technical standards. Open-source software demonstrated that voluntary cooperation across cultures could produce systems of astonishing sophistication. The internet did not abolish the nation-state, but it often operated according to a logic that transcended it.Many of the major technology companies genuinely believed they were extending that tradition. Their work forces became international and they acquired global user communities. Product launches were increasingly discussed as worldwide events rather than national ones. Executives frequently spoke in the language of humanity rather than citizenship, presenting their platforms as shared spaces that belonged, in some broader cultural sense, to everyone who used them. The distinction between an American company and a global institution became deliberately blurred. History, however, has a way of reintroducing distinctions that periods of optimism encourage us to overlook.The return of geopolitics over the past decade has been one of the defining developments of the twenty-first century. Strategic competition between major powers has expanded far beyond military capability to encompass semiconductors, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, undersea cables, quantum research and digital infrastructure. Technologies that were once understood primarily as commercial products have become matters of national security. Supply chains are scrutinized through strategic rather than economic lenses. Investment decisions increasingly reflect geopolitical calculations. Even the language has changed. Governments now speak of technological sovereignty, strategic autonomy, and digital resilience with a confidence that would have seemed unusual only a decade ago.The internet did not escape this transformation. For the technology companies themselves, this represented an unusually difficult moment. They had spent decades cultivating identities that rested upon universality. Their products connected families, businesses, and communities across political boundaries. Their legitimacy depended, at least in part, upon the perception that they served users rather than governments. Yet the world around them increasingly demanded choices that universal institutions rarely have the luxury of making.This is not a moral criticism. No corporation exists outside the legal and political framework of the state in which it is incorporated. Governments possess legitimate security interests. Companies have legal obligations. In periods of geopolitical stability, these realities often remain comfortably in the background; during periods of strategic competition though, they become impossible to ignore. What changed was not simply the relationship between governments and technology companies. It was the relationship between technology companies and the stories they had long told about themselves.The promise of universality became increasingly difficult to sustain once digital infrastructure itself became a strategic asset. A platform cannot simultaneously present itself as belonging equally to everyone while operating within a world that increasingly expects technological capability to serve national interests. The contradiction is not necessarily the fault of the companies involved; it is a consequence of history changing around them.There is a revealing parallel with another great infrastructure of modernity. For much of the twentieth century, commercial aviation cultivated an image of cosmopolitanism. Air travel compressed distance, encouraged cultural exchange, and embodied the optimism of an increasingly interconnected world. Yet no one seriously imagined that airlines existed independently of states. Routes reflected diplomacy. Airspace reflected sovereignty. Aircraft manufacturing reflected industrial strategy. The industry remained deeply international while never ceasing to be profoundly geopolitical.Digital platforms are discovering a similar reality. The internet encouraged us to believe that information could flow independently of power. For a time, perhaps it did. Today, information infrastructure has become power. Artificial intelligence depends upon computational capacity. Computational capacity depends upon semiconductor supply chains. Cloud services depend upon data centers, energy grids and legal jurisdictions. Networks remain global, but they are no longer politically weightless.This shift has consequences that extend well beyond geopolitics. For users around the world, one of the most striking aspects of the early internet was the feeling that participation itself conferred a kind of equality. A student in Addis Ababa, an entrepreneur in Mexico City, and a researcher in Helsinki entered the same digital spaces and, at least in principle, encountered the same opportunities to create, publish, and collaborate. The internet’s openness did not eliminate global inequalities, but it fostered the belief that the network itself belonged to no single political center.That belief has become harder to sustain. Increasingly, the largest digital platforms appear not simply as global companies headquartered in the United States, but as organizations whose strategic interests inevitably intersect with those of their home state. Again, this is not unusual in historical terms. It is precisely how most industries have always functioned. The novelty lies elsewhere. For perhaps the first time since the commercial internet emerged, the mythology of technological universalism has given way to the more familiar realities of geography, sovereignty, and power.The consequences are likely to endure long after today’s geopolitical tensions have evolved into new forms. Once users begin to see platforms not as neutral environments but as actors embedded within particular political and economic systems, trust acquires a different character. Questions that once appeared purely technical become constitutional. Who governs digital space? Whose values shape its rules? Whose interests ultimately prevail when cooperation gives way to strategic competition?These are not questions that engineers alone can answer. Nor, for that matter, are they questions that any platform can resolve through better product design. They belong to a different historical moment altogether.The great irony is that the internet has arrived at precisely the moment when the world is rediscovering the enduring importance of political boundaries. The dream that networks might quietly dissolve geopolitics has not survived contact with the twenty-first century. It is not the internet that failed but the assumption that technology could ever remain separate from history.Konstantinos Komaitis, PhD, is a veteran of developing and analysing Internet policy to ensure an open and global Internet.

item.title: Disney Offers $20 Million For Character.AI Assets As Startup Files For Bankruptcy
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Character.AI has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection and plans to sell substantially all of its assets, with Disney offering $20 million as a "stalking-horse bidder" for select intellectual property and company claims. However, the company said Disney's bid is subject to "higher or better offers." Deadline reports: The company, which allows users to create and interact with AI-generated avatars, said it made the filing in U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware. It said it hopes the process will allow it to "facilitate a value-maximizing sale of all or substantially all" of its assets. The Character.AI platform will continue to operate during the bankruptcy.
The Disney agreement, reached prior to the filing, would give the media giant a non-exclusive perpetual license of select intellectual property and company claims from Character.AI. Disney would pay $20 million and provide resources during a transition period as the company explores a sale. [...] Character.AI said it is aiming to conclude the sale process by late November or early December. Character.AI has faced a series of controversies over the past year or so. Most notably, the company settled multiple lawsuits alleging its chatbots encouraged self-harm and suicide among teenagers, including a high-profile case involving 14-year-old Sewell Setzer III.
The company also faces lawsuits from Kentucky, which alleges its chatbots encouraged self-harm, and Pennsylvania, which claims the bots illegally impersonated licensed doctors. The latter allegations follow earlier complaints that Character.AI's therapy chatbots engaged in the unlicensed practice of medicine.
In September 2025, Disney accused Character.AI of copyright infringement and using its characters in chatbots that were "sexually exploitive and otherwise harmful and dangerous to children," prompting their removal from the platform. These mounting legal challenges and regulatory scrutiny ultimately contributed to this eventual bankruptcy filing.

item.title: U.S. Car Privacy And Security Remain An Absolute Shitshow
item.author: Karl Bode
item.content:encoded: Despite a lot of noise and fury, the U.S. doesn’t do anything about this for the same reason we refuse to pass a modern privacy law or regulate data brokers: “we” (more accurately the people who purportedly democratically represent us) have repeatedly decided that making gobs of money is significantly more important that human lives, public safety, consumer privacy, or even national security.Consumer Reports is conducting a more recent follow up study in collaboration with Northeastern University. The full study will arrive next week, but their breakdown of what they’ve found indicates the problem hasn’t gotten better — and in some cases may have gotten worse.The researchers tested 21 vehicles and their companion mobile apps at CR’s Connecticut auto testing facility using a faraday cage to isolate and analyze vehicle communications. They found they funneled oceans of behavioral, driving, browsing, location, and other data to a long list of industries and companies. Often without fully informing consumers:“…almost a quarter of the vehicle apps were found to be sending out personally identifiable information, including vehicle owners’ names, vehicle identification numbers (VINs), and precise geographic locations. That information can make it easy for companies to link driving behavior to personal data profiles created by data brokers and marketers. Such profiles are routinely sold to banks, insurers, pharmaceutical companies, lenders, and retailers, who can use it for personalized loan terms and filtered bank and insurance offers, a CR and CalMatters investigation found.”Car makers, as they’ve always done, often blame third parties for any “data leakage” and act surprised when provided details on the width and depth of the data transfer. One company, Honda, claims it put an end to the problem immediately (which in a working country, regulators would independently confirm):“General Motors, Honda, Nissan, and Stellantis (which owns 14 auto brands, including Chrysler, Dodge, Fiat, and Jeep), said some recipients of driver data were prohibited from independently using or selling any data they are provided. But the Northeastern researchers found those restrictions aren’t necessarily effective: After they showed their findings to Honda, the company instructed one of its vendors, Amplitude, to delete all of the location data it had received and stopped sending it going forward.”In a lot of instances (much like the “smart TV” and other markets), if consumers try to take informed action to opt out of collection and protect themselves, they lose vehicle functionality. Again, carmakers do this because they know the federal U.S. government won’t meaningfully hold them accountable. And the government won’t hold them accountable because the current U.S. government is too corrupt to function in the public interest — and incentivized toward apathy because it unconstitutionally exploits this dysfunction to buy data and avoid warrants. But as we saw with the “TikTok ban,” this is all annoyingly performative. China doesn’t need TikTok, EVs, or Chinese-made drones to collect sensitive U.S. consumer data because they can already buy most of it on the open and largely unregulated market. And they can buy most of it on the open market because the U.S. Congress is too corrupt to function in the public interest, despite ample pretense to the contrary.

item.title: Ledger Confirms Spy Chip Implant Behind Wallet Crypto Thefts
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Longtime Slashdot reader AmiMoJo shares a report from BleepingComputer: Ledger has confirmed that some of its devices distributed through Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis were compromised with a hardware implant that drained users' cryptocurrency wallets. The company has been investigating reports of users losing funds from wallets purchased through CryptoBilis, a major Malaysia-based hardware wallet retailer operating across Southeast Asia. Some researchers have shown the implant in Ledger X since September 16, saying tampered devices were available for nearly half the price of the original hardware.
[...] In a report over the weekend, Tibane Labs notes that the threat actor made room for the malicious circuitry by replacing the original battery with a smaller one, which powers both the implant and the Ledger X. "Under the battery and antenna sits an ST STM32G431KBU6 (Arm CortexM4, 128 KB flash, UFQFPN32)," the researchers found inside one of the devices. For connectivity, the actor used "a tiny eSIM, an 8pad package just 2x2 mm, next to the MCU, and a shielded LTE module that sends the words out."
[...] Ledger is advising users to avoid purchasing from unauthorized resellers as they run an increased risk of getting counterfeit or modified devices. The company is also reminding its authorized resellers and distributors to get the products only through authorized channels and to avoid restocking returned products. Ledger provides a 'Genuine Check' mechanism to determine the authenticity of the device; however, it explicitly warns that it cannot detect added implants when the device's original Secure Element remains intact.

item.title: Trump Bans CNN, Then Has DOJ Investigate CNN For Not Covering Him
item.author: Mike Masnick
item.content:encoded: Remember when Elon Musk told advertisers to go fuck themselves… and then sued them (unsuccessfully) for not advertising on his personal propaganda and manipulation site? Well, it appears that Donald Trump is trying a government-backed variation on that abusive power play: claiming that news networks choosing not to cover him after he announced he was initiating a “free press ban” in the White House… is somehow an antitrust violation.The Justice Department is investigating whether the major television networks — ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News — violated federal antitrust laws when the group brieflysuspended their pooled coverageof President Trump, according to six people with knowledge of the department’s action.Officials from the Justice Department contacted networks on Friday and demanded communications and materials related to the White House TV pool, the people said. The pool is a longstanding system where the networks share the responsibility of providing footage of the president and distributing it to other news outlets.So, before we get into the details here, let’s just do a quick refresher of the same “antitrust 101” lesson I suggested for Elon Musk two years ago during his lawsuit. While there can be antitrust concerns when a group of businesses get together to engage in a boycott, that only applies to situations where that boycott is focused on actual harms to consumers or competition. A boycott with political and expressive aims is protected under the First Amendment, and publicity campaigns aimed at influencing government are not an antitrust violation. This has been established over and over again at the Supreme Court and beyond.Indeed, as former FTC chair William Kovacic tells the NY Times, the biggest missing factor here is that for there to be antitrust, there needs to be a commercial motive:“The critical ingredient in successful antitrust cases is to demonstrate that there is unmistakably a commercial motive and that the commercial motive predominates,” Mr. Kovacic said. “And I don’t think they would ever be able to do that here.”So this “investigation” is little more than fan service for the MAGA faithful in an attempt to create chilling effects on the media after Trump threw a hissy fit that the media wasn’t covering his every damn word as closely as before. The White House TV “pool” reporting involves a rotating group of media entities which share their work with others so that not every journalism org has to have their own camera crew (there are separate pools for radio and print, again to avoid overlap and crowding).As a reminder, on Friday, September 18th, Donald Trump announced that he was “banning the free press” from the White House, specifically in the form of pulling the press passes from CNN, Politico, and MSNow reporters. On Monday the 21st of September, CNN had been scheduled to handle the TV pool that day, but since it was barred, it didn’t do so. And the other members of the TV pool — ABC, CBS, NBC, and Fox News — all agreed they would not step in to cover for the White House’s clearly unconstitutional attack on CNN and the other media entities barred from the White House.Thus, for a few days there wasn’t TV pool coverage, which seemed to piss off Trump, even though it was all in response to his own First Amendment-violating censorial actions. He took to his own personal pinboard, Truth Social, to whine about the lack of coverage of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s state visit:CNN and MSDNC, to show you how fake they are, today refused to cover one of the Biggest and Most Beautiful Events to take place in many years, the arrival at the White House of the Highly Respected President of China, Xi Jinping, and his beautiful wife, Madam Peng. The event was magnificent—Actually made for Television but, because they’re Fake News, and because they knew how good it would be, they didn’t want credit to be given to ‘TRUMP,’ they refused to be there. That’s why they have such poor Ratings.Yes, that’s Donald Trump literally complaining that CNN and MSNow “refused to cover” an event days after he had personally banned them from the White House where the event was happening.The MAGA base, of course, quickly spun up nonsense claims about how not covering the president was clearly an antitrust violation (it’s not) with Laura Loomer attacking the current boss of the DOJ’s antitrust division, Stanley Woodward, as secretly a “Democrat.”Meanwhile, back in the actual story, by Thursday of that week a judge had granted a temporary restraining order against the White House, telling the White House to let the reporters back in. It took some time to do so, but eventually CNN, MS Now, and Politico reporters were given their WH press passes back, at least while the TRO remains in effect. And by Friday morning, September 25th, after just four days of no TV pool coverage, the networks restarted the press pool.The White House almost immediately tested the boundaries of the TRO by blocking CNN from Air Force One (claiming the TRO only applied to the White House itself) the very next day. CNN was scheduled to handle the TV pool for that Trump trip to Tennessee, so the pool went dark again directly because the White House barred CNN from the flight. That same day, however, the networks announced they would restart the TV pool coverage, just without CNN, effectively caving to the Trump White House.So, to sum up, the non-banned networks stood firm to boycott Trump’s TV pool for… five whole days (Monday through Thursday, and then Saturday) before totally caving and continuing to provide Trump pool coverage.But Laura Loomer called Stanley Woodward the worst insult you can imagine for a MAGA cultist: “a Democrat.” And thus there must be action to feed the culture war beasts. Hence… an investigation into the networks for refusing to run the TV pool for less than a week in response to Trump illegally banning one member of the pool, that, Trump complained, wasn’t covering him even after he had banned them.In a statement on Saturday, a Justice Department spokeswoman, Emily Covington, described the five networks as having “proudly boycotted covering White House events.”“Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act,” a core antitrust law, Ms. Covington wrote. “The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.”Again, as discussed above, that’s not at all how the Sherman Act works. And everyone involved knows that full well. The only purpose of this is to (once again) punish the press for its editorial choices — and possibly to get private insight into the networks’ editorial decision-making process as part of the investigation.I mean, it really needs to be emphasized here that the DOJ is investigating CNN for “boycotting” pool coverage it was literally banned from providing. In the MAGA cultist worldview, Donald Trump can ban whoever he wants from the “free press” but those he does not ban are absolutely required to cover him and spread his conspiracy theories and bullshit to the world.But these stories are all the same basic story: Trump has such a fragile but inflated ego that he believes news networks are required to cover him positively, and that he can punish news orgs that (1) don’t cover him positively or (2) don’t cover him at all.That’s not how the First Amendment works, but it is how the MAGA Trump world punishes news organizations for their editorial choices. But, of course, all the people who spent years screaming about “Biden admin censorship” are suddenly very, very quiet.

item.title: As Federal Court Rules ALPRs are Mass Surveillance, EFF Gets Disappointing Ruling
item.author: Andrew Crocker
item.content:encoded: In an extremely disappointing ruling, a California trial court dismissed , our case challenging the city of San Jose’s warrantless searches of its vast stores of automated license plate reader (ALPR) data. EFF and the ACLU of Northern California represent SIREN and CAIR California, two non-profits that serve San Jose residents, in this case.Make no mistake: We believe this ruling is wrong on the law, and we will appeal. The ruling ignores the importance of landmark rulings from the U.S. Supreme Court regarding the invasiveness of aggregating collected data on an individual over time, including one issued just months ago. It also severely underestimates the harm that ALPRs cause, in San Jose and around the country. San Jose’s ALPR surveillance system is inescapable. It blankets the city’s streets in nearly five hundred cameras that continuously photograph every car that passes by and retains the collected data for a month or longer. In our briefs, we argued that law enforcement officers who warrantlessly search the resulting ALPR database are violating the California Constitution’s ban on unreasonable searches and its guarantee of privacy. The court disagreed, explaining that based on one California appeals court case involving individual streetlight cameras, people do not have a reasonable expectation of privacy when driving on a public road. This is wrong. Networked ALPRs are not individual streetlight cameras. Their net effect of tracking and mapping cars as they travel reveals patterns of life, intimate relationships, and much more.Fortunately, there are signs that the tide is turning against ALPRs in the courts. Just a day before the ruling in our case, a federal district court in Oklahoma called ALPRs “a type of indiscriminate mass surveillance” and decided that a law enforcement officer’s warrantless search of ALPR data violated the Fourth Amendment. The officer was observing traffic on an Oklahoma highway when he saw a woman driving a car with California plates. According to the court order, the officer began following the woman “for no apparent reason” other than her out of state plates. While following her, the officer decided to run the woman’s license plate number through Flock’s ALPR system – again, with no apparent reason other than her California plates. The Flock search returned at least 30 days of data, allowing the officer to track the car across at least three states, over the span of a month, from a single search.The facts of this case demonstrate how ALPRs allow law enforcement to grab a breathtakingly vast sweep of information about a car (and the driver within) with no more effort than a Google search. It’s true that when a person drives on public roads, they can be observed, including by police. But as the Supreme Court hasexplained, we don’t expect law enforcement to be able to secretly track and store movement our cars while we’re driving. The federal court in the Oklahoma case aptly illustrated this difference in societal expectations:We might reasonably expect our friends and family to tell us something like: “Hey, I saw you out driving by the store last week.” But we do not expect people we know—let alone strangers, and especially not law enforcement—to randomly approach us to say: “Hey, I have been following your car for the last 30 days, and here is a detailed log of every place your vehicle has been with supporting photographic evidence. I am also going to share this information with law enforcement throughout the country so they know your whereabouts, too.This decision is the first of its kind, and EFF will continue working to ensure that it is the first of many. Outside the courts, we’ve seen people across the country step up to reject ALPRs at the state and local level. EFF will continue challenging this technology on every front as well.

item.title: FBI Arrests Canadian Cybersecurity Expert In ShinyHunters Hacking Case
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Canadian cybersecurity figures say they were shocked after ransomware negotiator Edward Dubrovsky was reportedly arrested in Pennsylvania in connection with the FBI's ShinyHunters hacking investigation. "We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what's left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate," wrote FBI Director Kash Patel on social media. CBC News reports: Reuters reported Sunday that sources familiar with the matter identified the arrested suspect as Ed Dubrovsky, a Canadian cybersecurity executive whose career has focused on helping clients negotiate with ransomware attackers. Court documents from the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania show Dubrovsky is facing two criminal charges: conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money, and interference with commerce by threats. The allegations have not been proven in court.
"For the cybersecurity community in general, I think that there's a sense of shock," Toronto-based tech and cybersecurity analyst Ritesh Kotak told CBC News on Monday. Kotak says Dubrovsky is "very popular" and has spoken at numerous conferences, but stressed that the charges "are clearly just allegations" and that it is not yet known "what exactly has happened." "This is an individual that was for the most part respected when it came to ransomware negotiations," he said. "A lot of people are familiar with his work as well." ShinyHunters is one of the world's most prolific data theft and extortion groups that's been tied to major campaigns, including a recent breach involving FBI employee data, a cyberattack on Canvas, as well as various cyberattacks affecting companies including Telus, Microsoft, and Ticketmaster.

item.title: The Creator of ‘Smutstep’ Wants You to ‘Let Your Freak Flag Fly’
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: Last week, a video came across my feed of a man saying horny lines over a dubstep beat. “On your knees,” he snarled. As the beat dropped, he growled, “Mmm, now look at me.” “Instagram reels just showed me a guy who makes 'smutstep' for the booktok crowd and it is the funniest thing I have ever watched,” the person reposting the video on X wrote. The replies are predictably harsh: “I think this is actually the worst thing I have ever heard.” “Who the FUCK is demanding this 😭” People demanding this is why it exists. , whose real name is James, is a dubstep musician and voice artist who’s been working in the music industry and voice acting world for years. But smutstep is what’s made his work go viral, in part thanks to the people who hate it so much – and the ones who demand more of it.Smutstep emerged as a reaction to , a subculture within TikTok built by book lovers and their various followings. Within BookTok, the romantasy book genre thrives, with series like and A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR) gaining massive readerships for their blend of elven high fantasy and dragon-based erotica. The romantasy genre is not a quaint fandom. It’s a .Like so many online communities devoted to things a little horny and misunderstood, the wider world tends to scrutinize and discredit romance readers, especially when Fae fucking is involved. James, who wants people to know he does read the books too, saw a way into two niches that could compliment each other.“I think what I like about the whole culture — the BookTok culture and dubstep culture — it's just letting your freak flag fly in a way,” he told me in a call. “It’s accepting and embracing what you're into within a safe and healthy space. I think that's a really beautiful thing.” James and I talked about modern artistry in a world where interactivity and engagement rule, why he doesn’t take all of this too seriously, and the value of escapism in a time when everything else sucks. And yes, I ask him to do the growl.This interview has been edited for length and clarity.SAM: I will admit just off the bat, I'm not in the BookTok world personally.I have nothing against BookTok. Beautiful community. But I can't get into it. I've tried like, . I haven't found my romantasy, I suppose. So I might ask you some dumb questions, but hopefully you can also serve as a little bit of an explainer for those of us who are not super in that world. Tell me how you got into this?Yeah. So the thing is, it wasn't like when I was a kid, I was like, when I grow up I wanna growl. You know? I've been a trained professional vocalist for a really long time. I've done metal and I've done theatre, I've done pop, I've done rock. The reason I'm in Nashville right now is because I spent eight years in a country band that was touring the world. I just kinda do everything there is to do with my voice. I've been a professional performer and vocalist for a really long time. My wife is really into the BookTok world. And so I was exposed to the community and the books through her. The first video that went viral for me was when I had just left my country band. And all I wanted was for the way I was presenting myself and expressing myself to be true to the things that I was into, which is dubstep. I had fallen in love with dubstep. I think it's the most beautiful community in the world. And then, I've always been a huge fantasy fan. I've always been really into and and all that stuff. So getting into romantasy was not a big step for me, because I'm already a fan of fantasy. Making that video was me kind of saying, ‘I feel like a lot of these BookTok boys are getting the growl wrong.’ And then I did a growl that I did from back in my metal days. And it just blew up and it created this whole community of people who were really into the growl. But I was not the first person to do the growl. There's another creator who was doing it long before me. His name's . I can't take credit for being the first to BookTok growl, but I definitely get a lot of recognition for it. Obviously I wanted to be producing dubstep music, but my community all wanted me to growl, so it was like, how do I make this make sense? And so I just started growling in my dubstep and inadvertently created a subgenre of dubstep called smutstep. It's all community driven though. Honestly, even the name smutstep was a comment on one of my videos.Somebody had requested that I growl ‘sit down’ and I did a video growling it that did really well. So I was like, well, let's just make a dubstep drop out of this. It's community driven, and it's fun. I'm glad that people are liking it. I think the biggest issue though is that... I'm having fun. I do not take this seriously. Again, it wasn't a dream of mine to grow up and growl at people. I took two very niche communities — the dark romance BookTok niche community, and the dubstep community — that are not designed to be exposed to general culture. So there's a lot of hate that comes with that and a lot of negativity. People react very strongly to what I do. And I think that that's as an artist, I think that's effective art. You want people to be moved to an extreme. You know? But you cannot control what that extreme is gonna be. There are people that treat me like Marilyn Manson in the nineties. His art is meant to be taken seriously. He is making a social commentary where he's putting a mirror up to society and showing how ugly it is. Whether you love that or you hate it, it's meant to be taken seriously. Smutstep is not meant to be taken seriously. If you enjoy it, that's awesome. You know what I mean? I'm having fun with it. I love the community I've created around it. We're all having fun. But it's not meant to be taken as seriously as so many of the haters take it. Yeah, it's broken containment from these specific niche communities, into the wider world. Which is the curse and blessing of social media, I guess. Something breaks out and becomes viral and then everybody's aware of it, even people who maybe are not the audience. I sent you the link to the video that's got a , and all the comments and replies are really rude. So just be warned. People are like, ‘I'm never gonna unmute this. I would never unmute this to save my life,’ that kind of thing. And like you said, it’s not that serious. If it's not your thing, that's okay. Move on.But what do you think about those comments? The ones that are like, ‘this is gigacringe.’That's been a lot of what I deal with on other platforms. Facebook and TikTok are way better. On Instagram, l have my comments limited to people who follow me because it's just so much hate. People are crazy on Instagram. People will say the most sideways shit on Instagram.Yeah, and that's that's the thing. Like obviously, as much as we're all just having fun, of course it does mentally take a big toll on you.You said this is community driven. Were people waiting to have this sort of thing enter their already-existing BookTok community, or where do you think it comes from? Why are people resonating with this?Men in BookTok is not a new thing. Making it dubstep is my brand. But for me, smutstep is like the KISS makeup. It's a gimmick. Everybody needs something that makes them stand out. So right now, smutstep is what makes me different, it's what makes me unique. Most of my content is based off of people making requests in the comments. I think that may be why it's taken off the way it has. Obviously it has to do with me, but it has so much to do with the people who are enjoying it. This is something that I think in a lot of ways is actually a much more modern take on entertainment. From its inception, it’s community demand, and giving people what they want within what I wanna do. I'm not doing something I don't wanna do. It's like, all right, you guys want this? Well, I'm gonna make it, but I'm gonna go the dark romance route and make it super aggressive, because I want to make dubstep out of it, and people are like, ‘That's fucking dope.’Are you familiar with like the romantasy theme park videos?Oh my god. You would get a kick out of this, and probably your wife would also, but it's part of SeaWorld. You know how around Halloween, theme parks will do like horror nights, and characters come out and chase you? It's that, but it's BookTok boys.. But it has gotten a really big reaction from wider culture, where people are like, ‘this is so cringe and weird.’ The execution really cringe and weird, but it is responding to something people wanted, which was: romantasy in a more interactive way. Is there anything that people are demanding from you more than other stuff? There's a book series called and there's a dragon in it called Tairn. Somebody said that Tairn should be Scottish, because his name is Tairneanach, which is a Scottish name. , but in the Scottish accent. I do another series with masked growls. I'm supposed to do one today, if the mask gets here in time. 'cause we're in spooky season, and people have been wanting that for as long as I've been doing this.I think what I like about the whole culture — the BookTok culture and dubstep culture — it's just letting your freak flag fly in a way. It’s accepting and embracing what you're into within a safe and healthy space. I think that's a really beautiful thing. Maybe it's just as I get older, but I'm just so disillusioned with reality and I constantly want more escapism for myself, and want to give others more escapism as well. So that's kind of my goal as an artist is just escapism.That’s a huge appeal of fantasy and romance in general. I'm also a big fan. That type of fantasy I can get with. I wonder if launched today, if we would be calling it romantasy. I guess there's not enough sex in it though.The thing about romantasy is, there does need to be pretty pretty graphic scenes in it. But has none of that. I do read the romantic stuff too. I don't wanna be somebody who just does it for the views. I do read both.Do you think people have picked up on the smutstep genre since you started? Are there new people doing it? I haven't noticed, but that doesn't mean someone's not out there trying and just hasn't had a video hit yet. And to be honest, I'm not surprised. I think that it's one of those things... It's human nature to have an aversion to something new that they don't understand. It’s still in the phase where I think it's more ‘what the fuck’ than something that is socially acceptable. Which again, it was never meant to be broadly socially acceptable. It was meant to be niche-acceptable, which it already is. I don't think there's a lot of people trying to do it because I think people are too afraid of having to deal with the same stuff I deal with.I would be remiss in letting you go if I didn't make you do a growl. Would you be willing to offer us a growl? I can. It's not going to be that loud, because I don't have a mic, but I can do one. Ready?Did you hear it? item.title: Jury Convicts Ohio Blogger Of Harassment For Sending A Naked Shrek Pic To A Local Politician
item.author: Tim Cushing
item.content:encoded: In today’s episode of “wtf,” we have a jury deciding a local blogger is a criminal because a local politician didn’t appreciate being sent a Shrek bereft of clothes to his cell phone. Morgan Trau of the Ohio Capital Journal has the (pathetic) details on this particular miscarriage of justice. An Ohio political blogger let out a surprised laugh as he was found guilty of harassment after he sent an explicit digitally altered image of the cartoon character Shrek to a powerful lawmaker.After just thirty minutes, eight Lake County jurors decided D.J. Byrnes was guilty of telecommunications harassment against state Sen. Jerry Cirino (R-Kirtland), after he sent him two taunting messages and a meme of Shrek holding his genitals.Laugh he should, although we both certainly wish the laugh had been provoked by the judicial dismissal of plainly vindictive prosecution. The alleged crime has real consequences: up to six months in jail and a $1,000 fine. Fortunately (I guess) for Byrnes (who runs a popular local-focused blog that routinely criticizes local MAGA-leaning officials), the judge only ordered him to pay court costs and a $200 fine. But that shouldn’t let State Senator Jerry Cirino off the hook. After all, he conjured all of this into existence by using his power and political connections to turn a naked Shrek jpeg into a criminal conviction.The lawmaker testified he directly called the local police chief, saying he wanted charges to be filed. Public records show Cirino called the judge who signed Byrnes’ arrest warrant a “good friend” in late April and donated at least $2,500 to her political campaign in 2016. It’s impossible to say whether a different judge would have handled this arrest warrant differently, but it’s certainly easy to assume there was some grease on the wheels when judge was given the chance to review the affidavit. Cirino is not to be trusted. Not only did he use his connections to turn an unwanted text message into a criminal act, but he pretended (in court!) that this was harassment because Byrnes sent the naked Shrek to his cell phone. Just because he is a politician doesn’t mean he deserves that on his private cell phone, Cirino added.Whether or not Cirino “deserves” to receive taunting messages and dick-stroking Shrek pics is a question that isn’t really answered by this verdict. But what’s no longer open for debate is whether or not Cirino has a “private” phone that’s more deserving of protections not normally afforded to public figures, like local politicians. He doesn’t. The state may not be paying for his cell service contract, but the number is anything but “private.” One of the main arguments the defense brought up was that this was official political business and free speech, citing examples of Cirino using his cell phone for public business, even allowing local newspapers to publish his number for constituents to reach him.It seems Cirino only likes to receive supportive messages from right-wing locals. What he doesn’t care for is criticism, taunts, and naked Shreks sent to him by people who don’t agree with his political actions or views. Since he’s already handed it out to the locals, I’m sure any enterprising search engine user should be able to find this supposedly “private” number.But I’m sure people aligned with Cirino’s right-wing views will find Byrne first, and engage in similar harassment in response to previous “crimes” that embarrassed GOP figures and the people they love. Here’s a choice bit from Byrne/The Rooster’s CV:And that’s why Cirino went after Byrne. He could have done nothing more than block Byrne’s number to end the alleged “harassment.” But he didn’t. He made a personal call to the police chief and somehow managed to get his criminal accusations presented to a “good friend” who also happened to be a local judge. Politicians like Cirino consider corruption to be a feature of government, rather than a bug directly related to citizens trusting their fellow Americans to serve their interests, rather than their own. Hopefully, the end result of this will be Cirino being voted out of office and those who aided and abetted his petty quest for revenge coughing up a settlement to Byrne for violating his rights.

item.title: Judge Orders Trump To Stop Airing Taxpayer-Funded Midterm Propaganda Ads (For Now)
item.author: Karl Bode
item.content:encoded: Last week, the DNC sued the Trump administration for using $20 million in taxpayer money on strange and ineffective midterm ads. The use of taxpayer money technically violates multiple laws (remember those?), including the Hatch Act and Federal Appropriations Laws restricting taxpayer-funded propaganda.1. On October 12, at 1:31 p.m. Eastern, the Washington Post reported that two ads continued airing after the Court issued the Order and into the early hours of Monday, October 12, on multiple programs, including “60 Minutes,” “ABC World News Tonight,” and “America’s Funniest Home Videos.” Ex. A.2. According to AdImpact data retrieved at 2:45 p.m. Eastern today, Defendants’ ads ran in nearly 400 spots on programs that began airing at 7 p.m. Eastern last night—that is, after this Court’s order was in effect. Ex. BThe Trump administration says it has already spent $19 of the $20 million allotted for the ads. In an attempt to pretend they weren’t breaking the law, the Trump administration falsely claimed that the propaganda efforts were “public service announcements” from US Customs and Border Protection — despite the fact that no government service or program was being advertised. On October 5 Trump responded to backlash by insisting he’d stop using taxpayer money for the ads and instead fund them via his SuperPAC. But not only is it not legal for Trump to direct his SuperPAC in such a fashion, he clearly lied and never actually stopped using taxpayer money to fund the ads, which continued to air.The TRO is scheduled to remain in effect for 14 days, and is “subject to an extension,” Rochon said. “Taking $20 million from a fund that Congress voted to use on border patrol, then spending it on vanity ads for an unpopular president, breaks the checks and balances set in the Constitution,” Common Cause said in statement. “If the Trump administration wanted to use money on personal promotional ads, they should have asked Congress to pass a bill to do so.”The grand irony is despite illegally stealing taxpayer money to fund the midterm ads, the ads themselves (several of which are just rehashed version of 2024 ads) are only likely to harm vulnerable Republicans now tethered to a disastrous war and Trump’s sinking health, polling, and political power.

item.title: After a 10-Year Redemption Arc, No Man's Sky Is Coming to the iPhone and iPad
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
No Man's Sky is coming to iPhone and iPad on October 28, more than a decade after its rocky launch and long-running redemption arc. The title will cost $19.99, but a free trial will let users try it out before purchasing. Ars Technica reports: It will run on devices as far back as the iPhone 11 and the third-generation iPad Air. No Man's Sky might not have the most cutting-edge AAA graphics (though they're still strong, and they've come a long way since launch via updates), but the game's uncommon method of generating galaxies of incomprehensible scale on device consistently for all players from a single-seed happening on a phone is remarkable for those of us who remember phones performing far behind consoles or desktop PCs.
This version of the game includes all of the content and systems updates to the game that have been added over the years -- the expansions that famously took the game from a rocky launch reception to a widely beloved redemption story. There are a couple of compromises, though, and it's similar to what we saw with No Man's Sky on the Nintendo Switch. Hello Games says the ability to build and explore player-made planetary settlements is limited to the iPhone 15 Pro and later, and multiplayer is not supported on any iOS device. "We are excited to see player feedback on iOS, and will support it appropriately based on how many folks are playing," the company says, leaving the door open to perhaps not supporting all future content updates if the player base isn't there to justify it.

item.title: A New 'Super Ice' Is 10 Times Stronger, Bringing It Close to The Strength of Concrete
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Researchers have created a strengthened "BioPykrete" by combining ice with cellulose nanocrystals and a custom protein that binds the plant-based crystals to the ice structure. In small-scale tests, the material was about 10 times stronger than regular ice and absorbed 70 times more energy before breaking. ScienceAlert reports: Instead of wood pulp's larger, disordered fibers, the researchers used cellulose nanocrystals here. Cellulose is the main structural material in plants, and in nanocrystal form, it can act as a microscopic strengthening agent for other materials, including ice -- essentially stopping cracks from spreading easily. The protein used here was called CBM3a-AFPIII, a combination of an antifreeze protein (AFP) and a carbohydrate-binding module (CBM). Its job was to act like glue, keeping the cellulose nanocrystals and ice bonded together.
It's a clever approach, and the researchers think that by tweaking their ingredients and methods, they might be able to improve their 'super ice' even further. "Optimizing solidification kinetics and freezing protocols, alongside developing diverse AFP-CBM variants, could yield even higher-strength composites," write the researchers. Besides further tests of the durability of the material, the researchers are also keen to take a closer look at how cracks propagate through BioPykrete, to confirm that the underlying strengthening mechanisms are what they think they are.
Further down the line, this approach could open up a whole new landscape for materials used in packaging, construction, and more: Using a custom protein to bring two unlikely compounds (ice and cellulose) together. "By bridging the gap between recombinant protein design and structural engineering, we have developed a high-performance material specifically engineered for the rigors of the world's most extreme environments," write the researchers. The findings have been published in the journal Colloids and Surfaces B: Biointerfaces.

item.title: Linus Torvalds On Why AI Works For Him
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from ZDNet: Many open-source developers still dislike AI. The latest example is System76 banning AI-generated content from its COSMIC desktop. At Open Source Summit Europe, Linux creator Linus Torvalds offered a different take: "I actually really like using AI," Torvald told Dirk Hohndel, his good friend and head of Ericsson Software Technology, in their latest discussion. [...] Torvalds said, "I think that you need to be very careful using AI when you're doing something real and important." Torvalds explained he hadn't always felt that way about AI programming. "I used to think it was just not very good -- but now I'm at the point where I actually really like using AI."
"To be fair," he continued, "I don't do a lot of kernel programming. I'm a maintainer. The Linux kernel is a project where other people do the real work, and I act as the collection point. But I still enjoy programming immensely. I think AI is a wonderful tool if you use it correctly and treat it as a tool, and I find it makes programming much more enjoyable." Torvalds recalled, "I started programming in 1981 or so, and back then computers were much simpler, and you could understand what they were doing, and also the programs you compared your own programs to were much simpler."
"It's a different story today," Torvalds said. "The bar in software engineering has grown so high that it's hard to see your own small efforts as worth anything, because you're used to all these polished, professional programs. [...] A lot of people make fun of vibe coding, but I think it's a wonderful way to find joy in programming. It makes you feel like you're doing something relevant. It allows you, as a new programmer, to do things that you would otherwise have a really hard time with."
He continued: "I love the concept of AI as a gateway drug because I was working on my own toy project, the guitar pedal, and I knew what I was doing. I had a user interface that I had written myself in C that was running on a microcontroller that was running on this small screen, and I was like, "This is just stupid. It looks like something from the '80s; I wanted it to look like something from this century. But I don't do Java. I do kernels." "So, I use AI to do the things that I'm bad at," Torvalds went on, "I'd seen all the same YouTube videos you have. Give AI a prompt, and it will do it. So I gave it a prompt, and it did it, and it was horrendous. Then I said, 'Hey, look! I already did this in C. I did it the right way. It's just ugly." Torvalds acknowledged that AI tools are helping identify security vulnerabilities and improve the Linux kernel, but at the cost of overwhelming maintainers with questionable bug reports and superficial fixes. He called some submissions "mindless band-aid kind of patches."
That said, despite AI's growing influence, Torvalds believes Linux's success comes from steady, incremental development rather than sweeping changes. "I'm a big believer in the whole incremental small changes that, over time, turn into big features," he said. The development goal remains "incremental improvement and steady progress all the time."

item.title: Firefox 158 Now Available With JPEG-XL Support By Default
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Firefox 158 is now available with JPEG XL image support enabled by default, making .jxl images a standard part of the browser rather than an experimental feature. The release also adds JPEG XL to Firefox's default image Accept header, improves Smart Window form filling, and brings new CSS typed-arithmetic support for developers. Phoronix reports: At long last, Firefox 158 is ready to go with JPEG-XL image support as an alternative to the likes of WebP, JPEG, PNG, and GIF. The default HTTP Accept header for image requests also now supports "image/jxl" for the JPEG-XL image format. Prior releases of Firefox had JPEG-XL gated by an experimental option.
Firefox 158 also now supports filling forms faster in Smart Window when clicking into a form field or selecting Fill from sources. On the developer side, CSS typed arithmetic are now supported to use functions like calc() to divide two values of the same data type even if of different units. Developer changes and release binaries can be found at their respective links.

item.title: Epic Games Delays Disney Project, Asks Developers To Use More AI
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Bloomberg: Epic Games delayed the release of an upcoming video-game collaboration with Walt Disney and told its developers to use more artificial intelligence tools to finish the game, according to people familiar with the project. The title had been slated for release in March, but is now delayed with no new date communicated, said the people familiar, who asked to not be identified because they weren't authorized to speak publicly.
Developers on the game, a shooter featuring characters from the Marvel and Star Wars franchises, were instructed to implement an "AI first" production model using tools such as Anthropic's Claude. Humans will then manage and guide that work. "No more hand-written code," one of the game's directors told staff in an internal message reviewed by Bloomberg. The director added that all art for the game would be "generated with full AI workflows."
Even before this announcement, the maker of the popular Fortnite game had been pushing hard for the use of AI across all of its divisions. But this is the first time a major video-game company has attempted to build a title primarily with AI. "We're embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do," said Jake Jones, communications director at Epic Games, in a statement to Bloomberg News.

item.title: Mark Zuckerberg Says Meta Has Reached AI 'Frontier', Rejects Calls For Slowdown
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says the company has reached the AI "frontier" with its new Muse Wonder model and will be offered as a closed, paid product for businesses. Zuckerberg also rejected calls for an industry-wide slowdown, arguing that AI can be managed with conventional guardrails as Meta continues spending heavily on models, infrastructure, and talent. The Financial Times reports: Speaking with the FT as Meta releases its Muse Wonder AI model on Monday, the billionaire chief executive claimed the new system was "going to allow much more sophisticated behaviours that are at the frontier of what is being done in the AI field." [...] "Getting to this point both required a large amount of compute and investment, and a lot of very rigorous scientific work by the group working on it over an extended period of time," said Zuckerberg. [...] Meta said Muse Wonder outperforms Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on some technical benchmarks. It said the new model can be used to carry out complex tasks from "understanding a lease to making sense of financial or health information." However, Muse Wonder will also be "closed," with its best versions sold directly to businesses. That pits it against Anthropic and OpenAI for corporate AI contracts in a serious test of its ambitions. Zuckerberg signaled further spending as Meta was "already working on the next step up," adding that its model development would "probably feel like it'll go quite a bit faster from here."
However, he also shrugged off mounting fears that the technology was advancing at a rate that will soon surpass human control. [...] The Meta chief declined to be drawn on his figure for "P(doom)" -- a much-discussed Silicon Valley term to describe the probability that AI will lead to mass destruction. Instead, he argued that responsibility should fall on the individual lab to ensure model safety. "I'm much closer to the belief that AI is a technology that can be engineered with normal guardrails and built responsibly than the anthropomorphic vision of AI, which is that it is just going to go do its own thing," he said. Zuckerberg has previously rejected calls by the heads of AI labs such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman for an industry-wide "slowdown" in AI development. He also played a key role in crafting US President Donald Trump's White House "Accord on Super Intelligence," setting out principles for self-regulation of the industry, which critics say falls far short of a formal global AI governance regime.
